FEB UNPAD Summer Program 2026 · 3 August 2026 · Bandung

The Growth We Want

Arief Anshory Yusuf

Bio

Arief Anshory Yusuf is Professor of Economics at Padjadjaran University, Indonesia, where he works on development economics. He is also Visiting Professor at King’s College London, Honorary Senior Lecturer at the Australian National University, and Non-resident Senior Research Fellow at UNU-WIDER. He holds a Bachelor in Economics from Padjadjaran University, an MSc from University College London, and a PhD from the Australian National University. He is a member of Indonesia’s National Economic Council (2024–2029), advising the President on strategic economic issues.

Inclusive, sustainable, and long overdue. We start with what is in the news — tariffs, trade barriers, an open world economy being dismantled — and with the politics that produced it. But underneath the politics is an economic root. Over the same decades the gains from growth stopped being shared, and that is what the backlash is answering — and what a better growth path has to deliver instead: broadly shared gains and a model the planet can actually sustain.

Where this goes

Seven movements

Every chart is built from primary data. Where a number is estimated, traced, or contested, the panel says so.

I

Where we are now

Start with what is in the news. The open trading order that defined the last forty years is being dismantled — tariffs, restrictions, and a world that has become harder to predict.

Protectionism returns

Trade stopped growing, and the barriers went back up

Slowbalization

World trade has stalled as a share of GDP since 2008

World Bank WDI, NE.TRD.GNFS.ZS, world aggregate, 1970–2024

Source & notes
Source: World Bank World Development Indicators, pulled live via the WDI API (country=WLD). Trade rose steadily from ~27% of world GDP in 1970 to a peak of ~61% in 2008, then plateaued and has oscillated in a band roughly 51–62% ever since — the "slowbalization" pattern: trade didn't reverse, but its multi-decade rise essentially stopped after the Global Financial Crisis.

Trade restrictions imposed worldwide have risen sharply

New trade-restrictive measures introduced worldwide per year

Goods

Source & notes
This is a traced estimate, not exact data — Global Trade Alert's raw figures remain behind an API credential this session doesn't have, so these values are read directly off the bar heights in IMF SDN/2023/001's Figure 7, the near-certain original source of the slide's chart (identical title "Trade Restrictions Imposed," identical Goods/Investment/Services breakdown, identical GTA sourcing). Total bar heights (read against the chart's 500-unit gridlines) are reasonably reliable: roughly 60–160 per year from 2009–2013, climbing through 650 by 2018, then accelerating sharply to ~980 (2019), ~1,380 (2020), ~1,900 (2021), and ~2,150 (2022). The Goods/Investment/Services split within each bar is a much rougher visual read and should be treated as illustrative, not precise — segment boundaries in a small stacked bar are hard to place exactly.

Geopolitical risk, same window as EPU

Geopolitical risk has climbed alongside economic policy uncertainty

Caldara & Iacoviello Geopolitical Risk Index (historical series), annual average, 2000–2025

Source & notes
Source: Caldara & Iacoviello, “Measuring Geopolitical Risk,” American Economic Review 112, no. 4 (2022) — historical index (GPRH, 1900–2019=100), built from the frequency of newspaper coverage of geopolitical tension, war, and terrorism. Pulled directly from the authors’ own public dataset (matteoiacoviello.com/gpr.htm). This is the sister index to the Trade Policy Uncertainty series in the same IMF report Figure 7 was traced from (IMF SDN/2023/001, Figure 6). Cropped to 2000–2025 to match the EPU chart alongside it. Visible spikes: 9/11 and Afghanistan (2001, 111), the Iraq War (2003, 135), and a sustained climb from 2022 (Ukraine, Middle East conflicts, tariff escalation) to 116 in 2025. For context, the fuller series (not shown here) reaches 200–380 during WWI/WWII — several times any level seen since. Today’s uncertainty is real and rising — but not, on this measure, unprecedented.

Peak of global uncertainty

Global Economic Policy Uncertainty is at historic highs

Baker, Bloom & Davis Global EPU Index, annual average of the monthly series, 2000–2025

Source & notes
Source: Baker, Bloom & Davis Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index, via FRED series GEPUCURRENT (GDP-weighted average of national EPU indices), monthly data averaged to annual here. The index spikes around 2008–09 (GFC), 2016 (Brexit/Trump), 2020 (COVID), and reaches its highest sustained level in the 2024–25 data.

II

The politics of it

Tariffs are not an economic accident — somebody voted for them. Across the democracies the same political turn has been under way for four decades.

Increase of right-wing populism

Far-right vote share has risen roughly ten-fold since the 1980s

Real election vote shares (ParlGov) classified by party family (PopuList), 30 European countries, 5-year averages

Source & notes
This is an original reconstruction, not a copy of the slide's exact category scheme. Built by merging two real datasets: ParlGov's actual national-parliament election vote shares (via parlgov.fly.dev, a working ParlGov mirror, after the main site's Cloudflare blocked direct access) with PopuList v4.0's party classification (far-right/far-left/populist flags with active-year ranges, matched on each party's parlgov_id). My classification rule, applied per party per election year: far-right if PopuList flags it far-right in that year; else far-left if flagged far-left; else "other populist" if flagged populist but not far-left/far-right; else mainstream. Vote shares are averaged in 5-year bins across all ~30 PopuList-covered European countries' national elections (636 elections, 1900–2023). Far-right vote share: ~1–2% through the 1970s–80s, rising past 10% by 2010 and reaching ~14% in the 2015–19 bin.

Ruling coalitions blend multiple parties differently across countries, so a country’s largest far-right party is not always in government even where it holds a large seat share (e.g. France, Germany).

Three explanations

Does inequality actually cause the backlash?

Each implies a different remedy.

1 · Economic insecurity

People left behind by the economy vote against it

The most widely-held view

Deindustrialisation, import competition and precarious work strip security from exactly the groups that swing to populist parties.

Inglehart & Norris themselves call this “perhaps the most widely-held view”, and note earlier work finding radical-right support concentrated among the unemployed, blue-collar workers and the less educated.

2 · Cultural backlash

It is about values, not wallets

Inglehart & Norris (2016); Norris & Inglehart (2018)

Support is a reaction by once-dominant groups against progressive value change — on immigration, gender, and national identity.

Testing both against European survey data, they find the model combining demographics with cultural values fits best. Adding cultural variables even makes the economic-insecurity effects reverse sign.

3 · Unfairness, not inequality

It is low mobility, not the size of the gap

Protzer, Harvard CID (2019, rev. 2021)

People accept unequal outcomes they consider fairly earned. They turn to populism when the outcomes feel undeserved.

Low social mobility correlates with the geography of populism within and across developed countries. Income and wealth inequality do not — and neither do immigrant share, social-media use, or the share of seniors.

Source & notes
Position 3 cuts against a simple “inequality → populism” claim: Protzer finds inequality levels uncorrelated with populism once mobility is accounted for. What survives all three accounts is narrower: whether people can get ahead matters politically — which is what the Great Gatsby Curve and the Lost Einsteins evidence measure. Sources: Inglehart & Norris, “Trump, Brexit, and the Rise of Populism”, HKS RWP16-026 (2016), Table 2 and surrounding discussion; Protzer, “Social Mobility Explains Populism, Not Inequality or Culture”, CID Working Paper 118, abstract.

III

The economic root

Underneath the tariffs and the votes is something economic. Over the same decades, the gains from growth stopped being shared.

Who actually gained from globalization · The Elephant Curve

Globalization’s gains went to Asia’s emerging middle class and to the global top 1% — the rich world’s lower-middle class got almost nothing

Annualized real income growth by global income percentile, 1988–2008 — Lakner & Milanovic's World Panel Income Distribution. Around the 56th percentile incomes grew +3.2%/yr, and at the very top +1.7%/yr — but at the 85th percentile, the working and lower-middle class of rich countries, growth was −0.3%/yr. That group is the “trunk” — and the constituency behind the populist turn shown above.

Source & notes
Built from scratch, not traced from Milanovic's published image: real country-decile income and population data from the World Bank's Lakner-Milanovic World Panel Income Distribution dataset (mysample==1, benchmark years 1988 and 2008; 750 country-decile observations in 1988, 1,209 in 2008, covering 4.1–6.1 billion people). Every country-decile pair was pooled, population-weighted, and ranked globally by income to build the 1988 and 2008 global income distributions independently, then linearly interpolated to whole percentiles 1–99 to compute each percentile's annualized real growth rate. Because deciles (not finer percentiles) are the finest grain available per country, this is smoother/coarser than Milanovic's original 100-bin version but reproduces the same shape: strong growth (2–3%/yr) through the emerging-economy middle of the distribution (largely China, India, and other Asian economies), a real dip to roughly flat or slightly negative around the 80th–85th global percentile (the "elephant's trunk" — rich-country lower-middle classes), then a renewed rise into the global top percentiles.

Whose data this is

Branko Milanović

Photo: Niccolò Caranti, Festival dell’Economia di Trento, 2018 · CC BY-SA 4.0

Serbian-American economist, b. 1953 in Belgrade. Former lead economist in the World Bank’s research department, where he spent about two decades; now at the Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality, City University of New York.

He is the economist who made global inequality — inequality between all individuals on earth, rather than within or between countries — a measurable subject, by assembling household surveys from across the world into a single distribution. The chart alongside comes from that work: the World Panel Income Distribution he built with Christoph Lakner, whose 1988–2008 growth-incidence curve became known as the “elephant curve.”

Books include Global Inequality (2016), Capitalism, Alone (2019) and Visions of Inequality (2023).

The long view · 1820–2024

Top 1% income share, the full WID history: 1820–2024

The same nine countries, extended back to the earliest year on record

Source & notes
Source: World Inequality Database, series sptinc992j (share of pretax national income, equal-split adults), percentile p99p100, same pull via WID.world’s official wid R package as the chart above. Coverage this early is sparse (a handful of benchmark years per century, reconstructed from historical tax and wealth records) and lower-confidence than the dense post-1980 data — treat the pre-1900 portion as indicative of the broad level and trend, not a precise annual series. Density picks up from the early 20th century onward as income-tax records begin, and becomes near-annual from the 1980s.

Why the mid-century compression, and why it lasted:
Shock (1929–45): Depression destroyed capital income (dividends/profits, most of the top 1%) faster than wages; WWII added >90% top tax rates, wage controls, and — especially in Germany, France, Japan — physical/financial destruction of capital.
Why it held for 30 years, not just wartime: peacetime govts kept top rates near 90% into the 1960s–70s; Bretton Woods capital controls (1944–71) kept finance small; unions stayed strong, keeping bargaining power with labor.
Why it reversed post-1980: tax cuts (Reagan/Thatcher era), capital-account liberalization, and de-unionization removed all three props at once.

Whose data this is

Thomas Piketty

Photo: Gobierno de Chile, 2015 · CC BY 2.0

French economist, b. 1971. Professor at the Paris School of Economics and the School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences (EHESS). The economist most responsible for putting income and wealth inequality back at the centre of the field, largely through Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) — a rare economics book that became a global bestseller.

That book grew out of a research program he started in the early 2000s with Emmanuel Saez: reconstructing top income shares from historical tax records, initially for France and the US, back to the early 20th century. Extending that method to more countries and longer spans, with Saez, Gabriel Zucman and others, produced the World Inequality Database (WID.world) — the top-income-share series used throughout this deck — which he co-founded and now co-directs at the World Inequality Lab.

That evidence base has fed directly into policy: progressive wealth-tax proposals in several countries, the OECD/G20 push for a global minimum corporate tax, and the EU Tax Observatory, which he helped found to track tax avoidance and inequality across Europe.

Other books include Capital and Ideology (2019).

Wealth and mobility

Wealth is more concentrated than income — and where the gap is wider, children inherit their parents’ position more tightly

World Inequality Database, 2024

Wealth is far more concentrated than income

Top 1% share of wealth vs. of pre-tax income

Wealth
Income
Source & notes
Source: WID.world, series shweal (wealth) and sptinc (pre-tax income), percentile p99p100, equal-split adults. All values are 2024 — no year-mismatch between countries. Wealth is concentrated 1.2–2.5× more than income everywhere in the sample. This is the mechanism behind Piketty’s argument profiled earlier: returns accrue to whoever already owns the assets, so wealth compounds ahead of wages.

Corak (2013), JEP 27(3), Figure 1

More unequal countries have less mobility

Intergenerational earnings elasticity vs. income inequality a generation earlier — higher means your parents’ income predicts yours more strongly

Source & notes
Source: Corak, “Income Inequality, Equality of Opportunity, and Intergenerational Mobility,” Journal of Economic Perspectives 27(3), 2013, Figure 1. Coordinates extracted from the paper’s own vector figure and verified point-by-point against the rendered original — all 13 countries match exactly. How to read it: the vertical axis is the elasticity between a father’s earnings and his son’s. At 0.15 (Denmark) almost none of your parents’ advantage passes to you; at 0.50 (UK, Italy) about half does. Caveat: this is a cross-country association, not proof that inequality causes immobility — and Corak adjusts published estimates for methodological differences, so treat individual country positions as indicative rather than precise.

IV

Why inequality rose

The gap did not open by accident. It opened where the gains from work were captured — and for most of the world, work was never formal to begin with.

The great decoupling

Productivity has outpaced compensation since the late 1990s

OECD Compendium of Productivity Indicators 2018, Figure 5.5 StatLink data, unweighted average of 20 OECD countries, 1995–2016

Source & notes
Source: not a re-derivation this time — this is the actual OECD StatLink Excel file behind Figure 5.5 of the OECD Compendium of Productivity Indicators 2018 (http://dx.doi.org/10.1787/888933734303), which every chart/table in that publication carries at the bottom of the page. Averaged here (unweighted) across all 20 countries in the figure: Australia, Belgium, Canada, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Korea, Latvia, Netherlands, Poland, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, UK, US. By 2016, GVA per hour worked (productivity) reached 152.9 (1995=100) while CPI-deflated compensation per hour reached only 140.8 — the gap between the two lines is the "decoupling."

Who got the gains

Labour stopped capturing the gains — in rich countries, and in most of the world

Penn World Table 10.0

Labour’s share of income fell in two-thirds of countries

Labour share of GDP, 1980–2019 · 86 of 133 countries fell, median −2.6pp

Source & notes
Source: Penn World Table 10.0, variable labsh. The median line is across all 133 countries with full 1980–2019 coverage; the named countries are shown to give the range. 86 of 133 (65%) fell, median change −2.6pp. India is the largest fall in the sample (−21.5pp); Indonesia (+1.9) and Brazil (+6.3) rose, so this is a strong tendency rather than a law. The ILO series via Our World in Data, an obvious alternative, begins in 2004. Over that window only 35% of countries fell and the median was positive — the series starts after most of the decline had happened, and its extremes are dominated by oil economies (Libya +33pp, Venezuela −29pp). The longer PWT window is the right test, and the shape of these lines shows why: most of the movement is before 2005.

Job polarization · 16 countries

Every one of 16 countries hollowed out its middle

Change in employment share by wage tier, 1993–2010, sorted by size of the middling decline

High-paying
Middling
Low-paying
Source & notes
The decline is universal: 16 countries, 16 shrinking middles, from Ireland (−14.9pp) to Portugal (−4.9pp). No country in the sample bucks it, which is the reason to treat polarization as a common technological phenomenon rather than the product of any one country’s labour-market institutions or politics. High-paying shares rise everywhere; low-paying shares rise in 14 of 16 (Finland and Luxembourg are the exceptions). Source: Goos, Manning & Salomons, “Explaining Job Polarization: Routine-Biased Technological Change and Offshoring,” American Economic Review 104(8), 2014 — extracted from the paper’s own appendix tables. Occupations are grouped into three tiers by mean European wage; “middling” is the 9 middle-wage occupation groups. European Labour Force Survey data, hours worked, 1993–2010.

The driver · routine-biased technological change

The jobs that vanished were the routine ones, not the low-skilled ones

Routine Task Intensity vs. change in employment share, 21 occupations, 1993–2010

High-paying
Middling
Low-paying
Source & notes
This is the mechanism, and it explains the shape. The Routine Task Intensity index (Autor & Dorn) measures how far an occupation consists of codifiable, rule-following tasks — the kind a computer can be programmed to do. It runs from −1.52 (managers of small enterprises) to +2.24 (office clerks). The fitted line is downward-sloping: the more routine an occupation, the more employment share it lost. Crucially, routineness is not the same as low skill. Personal and protective service workers are low-paid but non-routine, and grew the most of any occupation in the sample (+2.4pp); office clerks are middle-paid but highly routine, and fell 2.1pp. That is why computerization hollowed the middle rather than simply displacing the bottom — and why more education was an effective response. Source: Goos, Manning & Salomons, “Explaining Job Polarization: Routine-Biased Technological Change and Offshoring,” American Economic Review 104(8), 2014 — extracted from the paper’s own appendix tables. Occupations are grouped into three tiers by mean European wage; “middling” is the 9 middle-wage occupation groups. European Labour Force Survey data, hours worked, 1993–2010.

The inversion

Computers automated the middle. Generative AI points at the top.

Then · 1993–2010

Computerization pointed at the middle

Routine Task Intensity by wage tier — highest in the middle

Source & notes
Employment-weighted mean Routine Task Intensity for each wage tier, using 1993 hours-worked shares. The shape is an inverted U: routineness is concentrated in middle-wage work (+0.69) and negative at both ends — low-paying service work (−0.08) and high-paying professional work (−0.72) are both non-routine, for completely different reasons. That is precisely why computerization produced polarization rather than a simple top-versus-bottom split, and why moving up the wage ladder was a viable escape. Employment change follows directly: middling −9.3pp, low-paying +3.7pp, high-paying +5.6pp. Source: Goos, Manning & Salomons, “Explaining Job Polarization: Routine-Biased Technological Change and Offshoring,” American Economic Review 104(8), 2014 — extracted from the paper’s own appendix tables. Occupations are grouped into three tiers by mean European wage; “middling” is the 9 middle-wage occupation groups. European Labour Force Survey data, hours worked, 1993–2010.

Now · 2023

Generative AI points at the top

Share of an occupation’s tasks exposed to LLMs, by education required — highest at the top · exposure, not predicted job loss

Source & notes
What this measures, and what it does not. Source: Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin & Rock, “GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models” (2023), Table 6. Bars show the β measure — the share of an occupation’s tasks for which an LLM or LLM-powered software could cut the time to complete by at least half at the same quality — averaged within each O*NET job zone. This is an assessment of technical overlap between the tool and the work, made by human annotators and GPT-4 reading task descriptions. It is not a measure of job losses, wage effects, or employment change, and nothing in it has happened yet. The paper’s broader ζ measure, which assumes a fuller ecosystem of LLM-powered tooling, puts the bachelor’s tier at 71% rather than 47%; I use the more conservative β.

Why it matters next to the panel on the left. Routine task intensity peaks in the middle; LLM exposure rises with education and pay, peaking at bachelor’s-degree work (47%, roughly eight times the least-educated tier) before easing slightly at master’s-and-above (43%). The two gradients point at different parts of the distribution. Computerization hollowed the middle but left the graduate top growing, which is why “get more education” was effective advice; this technology’s overlap is greatest exactly where that advice led.

The serious counter-argument. Exposure is not destiny. Autor and others argue AI may complement expertise — letting less-credentialed workers do higher-value work and rebuilding a middle rather than hollowing a top; early studies find AI assistance helps lower-performing workers most. Whether the outcome is compressing or widening depends on who owns the technology, how the gains are taxed, and whether it is deployed to augment or to replace — which is a policy question, not a technological one. Comparability caveat: the left panel is Western Europe 1993–2010 and measures realised employment change; this one is the US in 2023 and measures potential. They are not two points on one series.

The double gap

For most of the world the question is not which jobs are shrinking — it is whether work is formal at all

ILOSTAT, latest year per country

Most of the world works without a contract

Informal employment, % of total employment

Source & notes
Source: ILOSTAT indicator SDG 0831, both sexes, all sectors, latest year available per country. Same countries and same order as the social-protection panel alongside, so a country can be tracked across both. The job-polarization evidence covers 16 Western European countries. For most of the world the labour-market question is not which tier of formal jobs is shrinking but whether work is formal at all. Brazil and South Africa are excluded: both report informality near 35%, far below other middle-income countries, because their labour statistics classify a much larger share of own-account and domestic work as formal — a definitional difference rather than a real one, and including them would mislead.

ILO, SDG indicator 1.3.1

…and most are not covered by the state either

Population covered by at least one social protection benefit, %

Source & notes
Source: ILO, SDG indicator 1.3.1, mostly 2021–23. Same countries and order as the informality panel. Read as a pair, these give the double gap: no protection through employment, and often none through the state either. Indonesia is 81% informal with 54% covered; Nigeria 93% and 15%; Kenya 86% and 9%. This is the evidence base behind the recommendation to invest in social protection — it is not that existing systems are failing, but that for most people they barely exist.

V

Growth stopped delivering

Even where growth continued, it did not always deliver what people actually wanted — and the planet is keeping its own account.

Robert F. Kennedy · University of Kansas, 18 March 1968

“Except that which makes life worthwhile”

Two decades before GPI or any formal GDP alternative existed, this was already the critique

“But even if we act to erase material poverty, there is another greater task, it is to confront the poverty of satisfaction — purpose and dignity — that afflicts us all. Too much and for too long, we seemed to have surrendered personal excellence and community values in the mere accumulation of material things.

Our Gross National Product, now, is over $800 billion dollars a year, but that Gross National Product — if we judge the United States of America by that — that Gross National Product counts air pollution and cigarette advertising, and ambulances to clear our highways of carnage. It counts special locks for our doors and the jails for the people who break them. It counts the destruction of the redwood and the loss of our natural wonder in chaotic sprawl. It counts napalm and counts nuclear warheads and armored cars for the police to fight the riots in our cities. It counts Whitman’s rifle and Speck’s knife, and the television programs which glorify violence in order to sell toys to our children.

Yet the gross national product does not allow for the health of our children, the quality of their education or the joy of their play. It does not include the beauty of our poetry or the strength of our marriages, the intelligence of our public debate or the integrity of our public officials. It measures neither our wit nor our courage, neither our wisdom nor our learning, neither our compassion nor our devotion to our country — it measures everything, in short, except that which makes life worthwhile. And it can tell us everything about America except why we are proud that we are Americans.”

Source & notes
Verbatim transcript of the delivered remarks (not the earlier prepared-text version, which differs slightly in places), University of Kansas, Lawrence, 18 March 1968, hosted by the Center for American Progress. Portrait: Harry Warnecke, New York Daily News, 3 September 1964 — public domain (published without copyright notice); the same file Wikipedia itself uses as RFK’s infobox portrait.

Kubiszewski et al. (2013)

Economic growth doesn’t guarantee an increase in life satisfaction

GDP per capita vs. reported happiness, 8 rich countries, indexed to the mid-1980s = 100

GDP per capita (annual)
WVS happiness (survey waves)
net change since first wave (red = fell, green = rose)
Source & notes
Tests, rather than assumes, the paper’s claim — built independently from real data, not traced from their figure. GDP per capita: World Bank (constant 2015 US$). Happiness: World Values Survey “happy/not happy” question, the same measure Kubiszewski et al. cite (Diener et al. 1999; Inglehart 2000), via Our World in Data’s WVS-vs-Gallup compilation; survey waves only (points shown), not annual. Verdict: mostly holds up. GDP per capita rose 47–94% across these 8 countries since the early-to-mid 1980s, while WVS happiness was flat or fell in 5 of 8 (Netherlands, UK, Denmark, USA declined; France flat); it rose modestly in Belgium, Germany and Italy, though Italy’s reading swings by ±10 points between waves with no clear trend. Caveat: a different wellbeing question gives a different answer. Eurobarometer’s “satisfied with life” measure, asked annually in these same countries since 1973, shows a clear rise in every one of them over the same decades — a reminder that “has life satisfaction risen?” can depend on which survey question is asked, not just which country or period.

This is a modern data point in the Easterlin paradox (Easterlin, 1974; cited directly by Kubiszewski et al. via Easterlin, 1995) — the classic finding that happiness doesn’t rise with GDP growth within a country over time, even though richer countries report higher happiness cross-sectionally. No single explanation is agreed on; candidates include: relative income (wellbeing tracks income relative to peers, so shared growth leaves relative rank — and happiness — unchanged); hedonic adaptation (people adjust to a higher income within months, resetting the baseline); rising aspirations (what people feel they need grows alongside what they have); positional goods (status competition is zero-sum, so growth in it can’t raise aggregate wellbeing); and growth’s uncounted costs — longer work hours, eroded social trust, pollution, crime — which is literally what GPI subtracts from GDP. A distributional version needs no psychology at all: if growth is captured disproportionately by top earners, median lived experience can stagnate while mean GDP keeps rising. Counter-argument: Stevenson & Wolfers (2008) find wellbeing does rise with income, just logarithmically, so a 40-year doubling of GDP implies only a small wellbeing gain that can be swamped by survey noise — and several of these countries (Netherlands, UK, Denmark) were already near a 90–95% happiness ceiling in 1984, leaving little room to rise regardless of income.

Does the same pattern hold in developing countries?

Growth and happiness move together for some, apart for others

GDP per capita vs. reported happiness, 8 populous developing countries (4 rising, 4 falling), indexed to 2011 = 100

GDP per capita (annual)
Happiness (Cantril Ladder, annual)
rose
fell
Source & notes
GDP per capita: World Bank (constant 2015 US$). Happiness: Gallup World Poll Cantril Ladder (0–10 scale), via the World Happiness Report series, 2011–2024. Countries selected on two rules at once: among the more populous, more widely recognized developing economies tested (100M–1.44B people), and split evenly — 4 where happiness rose alongside growth, 4 where it fell — rather than chosen to fit an answer either way. Result: genuinely mixed. China (+109% GDP, +26.5pp happiness) and the Philippines (+62%, +26.6pp) show the strongest gains in the whole set; Egypt (+28% GDP, −21.3pp happiness) and Bangladesh (+95%, −19.9pp) show growth with no happiness payoff at all. Across all 15 developing countries tested (not just these 8), the correlation between GDP growth and happiness change is weakly positive (r = +0.33) — the opposite direction from the rich-country panel, where the relationship was flat or negative in 5 of 8. Two reasons this doesn’t simply confirm or refute the rich-country finding: this window is 13 years, a third as long as the 40-year rich-country series, so there is much less room to separate a real trend from noise; and it spans COVID-19, a global happiness shock unrelated to income growth that hit some of these countries (Egypt, Bangladesh, Myanmar) harder than others. A plausible reading consistent with both panels: happiness rises with income mainly at lower income levels and flattens out at higher ones (Stevenson & Wolfers, 2008) — so growth’s payoff to wellbeing is real but not automatic, and clearly not guaranteed by growth alone.

The scissors

Since 1978, GDP per person rose 62%. Genuine progress didn’t move.

US GDP per capita vs. Genuine Progress Indicator per capita, constant 2000 dollars

GDP per capita
GPI per capita
Source & notes
Source: Table 1, The Genuine Progress Indicator 2006, Talberth, Cobb & Slattery (Redefining Progress), extracted from the published appendix and validated against the report’s own stated figures (GPI $1.31tn in 1950 and $4.42tn in 2004; GDP per capita $11,672 and $36,596 — all reproduce exactly). Why this edition: its per-capita series is internally consistent — GPI total ÷ population reproduces the published per-capita figure — whereas the 2004 edition’s per-capita column does not, so the two editions’ per-capita numbers are never mixed here. GPI per capita peaks in 1983 at $15,232 and is $15,036 in 2004; over 1978–2004 it moves −0.8% while GDP per capita rises +62.4%. Caveat: Dietz & Neumayer (2006) argue this threshold shape is partly baked in by GPI’s treatment of cumulative resource-depletion and long-term environmental costs; the 2006 authors respond that they replaced several assumed growth rates with actual data. Treat the flattening as a serious finding under contested methodology, not a settled measurement.

What grew faster than the economy

The costs GDP ignores grew faster than GDP itself

Growth multiple of each cost the GPI subtracts, 1950–2002, vs. GDP per capita’s 3.0×

Source & notes
Source: my own extraction of Appendix A, The Genuine Progress Indicator 1950–2002 (2004 Update), Redefining Progress (Cobb, Talberth et al.), cross-checked for internal consistency — the published GPI total reconciles with the sum of its components to within ±$2bn in every year tested. All figures in billions of 1996 dollars; growth multiple = 2002 value ÷ 1950 value. Bars are the costs GPI subtracts from consumption; the dashed line is GDP per capita’s own 2.99× growth over the identical period, so every bar to its right is a cost that outpaced the growth meant to justify it. Ozone depletion’s bar is clipped — its true multiple is 105×, off the scale, reflecting that this cost was near zero in 1950 rather than an explosion in absolute terms. Air pollution (0.6×) is the one cost that actually fell, largely thanks to the Clean Air Act — a reminder these are policy outcomes, not inevitabilities. Household pollution abatement is omitted: its 1950 value is zero, so no multiple exists.

Vogel & Hickel (2023), Lancet Planetary Health

Even “green growth” success stories fall far short of 1.5°C

CO₂ emissions in the 11 high-income countries that achieved absolute decoupling, each as % of its own 2022 level

Achieved (bold=avg, thin=each country)
Business as usual
1.5°C fair-share (my approximation)
Source & notes
An attempted, not exact, reproduction — built independently, not traced from their image. Like the original, this plots all 11 countries individually (thin lines) plus the population-weighted average (bold): Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Sweden, UK — the only Annex-1 countries (of 36 assessed) the paper finds with sustained absolute decoupling of consumption-based CO₂ from GDP, 2013–19. Data: GDP (World Bank, constant 2015 US$) and consumption-based CO₂ (Global Carbon Project, via Our World in Data), the same sources the paper itself uses. Validation: my population-weighted mitigation (CO₂ decline) rate for 2013–19 comes out to 1.66%/yr — the paper reports 1.6%/yr. Per-country decoupling rates run a bit higher than the paper’s (e.g. UK: I get 2.9%/yr mitigation vs. their 3.1%/yr), most likely because they use a 3-year moving average at each end of the 2013–19 window to smooth year-to-year noise, while mine uses raw endpoint years. Each country’s fair-share pathway is a genuine simplification: I allocated the IPCC AR6 remaining carbon budget (500 GtCO₂ globally from 2020, 50% chance of 1.5°C) by that country’s own population share, subtracted its actual 2020–21 emissions, then fit a simple exponential decay to what remains — not the paper’s published Raupach-curve method, whose exact parameters I don’t have. The qualitative pattern matches theirs: every country’s achieved reductions and BAU trajectory sit far above what a fair 1.5°C pathway would demand, and countries with lower per-capita emissions (Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark) have noticeably more room than high per-capita emitters (Australia, Canada, Belgium) — the same ordering the paper reports.

World Inequality Database, 2019

Who is actually causing this

Per-capita greenhouse-gas footprint by income group, tonnes CO₂e per person per year — log scale

Bottom 50%
Top 10%
Top 1%
Source & notes
Source: WID.world indicator lpfghg, per-capita greenhouse-gas footprint by income percentile, 2019. Read the axis carefully: it is logarithmic, because the range runs from 0.9 to 198 tonnes and a linear axis would compress everything below the US top 1% into a single line. Each doubling of distance along the axis is a tenfold increase. What it shows: the gap within countries is often larger than the gap between them. Indonesia’s top 1% emit 38.7t each — more than the average American (21.1t) — while Indonesia’s bottom half emit 1.6t. The US top 1% emit 225× a bottom-half Nigerian. Climate responsibility is not simply a rich-country/poor-country divide; it tracks income everywhere.

VI

What to do instead

None of this was inevitable. Each piece of it was chosen, which means each piece can be chosen differently.

A turning point in both countries

Ideology may have a role — so countries should choose theirs carefully

Inequality bottomed out in 1978, in both countries, and then the politics changed · Top 1% share of pre-tax national income, United States and United Kingdom, 1950–2024

United States
United Kingdom
Source & notes
What the data shows. Source: WID.world (World Inequality Database) via its official R package — the same series used earlier in this deck, re-cut to 1950 onward. Both countries’ top 1% share reaches its post-war minimum in the same year, 1978 (UK 6.64%, US 10.35%), and in both the trend reverses sign immediately afterwards: the UK ran at −0.10 pp/yr over the preceding two decades and +0.22 pp/yr through Thatcher’s tenure; the US ran at −0.09 pp/yr before and +0.50 pp/yr through Reagan’s. Over their terms the top 1% share rose +2.5pp in the UK and +4.0pp in the US — about +37% and +38% in relative terms.

What it doesn’t show. This is timing, not causation, and the chart cannot settle the question on its own. Several things arrived in the same window and are hard to separate: top marginal tax cuts, financial deregulation, de-unionization, the end of Bretton Woods capital controls, and the beginnings of the China trade shock. Inequality also rose in countries that had neither leader — generally later and less steeply — which argues against a purely Anglo-American political story. The honest reading is that the policy turn was real and consequential, but it ran alongside structural forces rather than simply causing the reversal. What the coincidence does suggest is that the post-war compression was not a natural equilibrium the economy would hold on its own: it rested on policy choices, and when the governing ideology about those choices changed, the direction changed with it.

Why this matters for choosing. If distributional outcomes were purely the product of technology and trade, governments would be passengers. This chart suggests they are not. The same global forces — computers, containers, China — hit every rich country, yet the countries that kept progressive taxation, strong bargaining institutions and universal services saw far milder increases in top shares than the two that most decisively abandoned them. That is the case for treating economic ideology as a live choice rather than an inevitability: it sets how the gains from growth are shared, and its effects compound over decades and are slow to reverse. A country picking a growth model is also picking who that growth is for — which is an argument for choosing deliberately, and for judging the choice against inclusion and sustainability rather than the headline growth rate alone.

Portraits. Reagan: official White House portrait, Michael Evans, 7 February 1981 — public domain as a work of the US federal government. Thatcher: stock portrait released by the Thatcher Estate for unrestricted use including commercial use and modification (the image Wikipedia itself uses); it dates from the mid-1990s rather than her years in office, as no freely-licensed 1980s portrait is available.

Not the size of the state — its progressivity

Inequality took off when the state’s redistributive role was cut back

Top marginal income tax rate and top 1% share of pre-tax national income, United States and United Kingdom, 1950–2017 · government spending shown faintly behind

Top marginal income tax rate
Top 1% share of pre-tax income
Government spending, % of GDP
Source & notes
The mechanism is progressivity, not size — and the distinction matters. Sources: top marginal income tax rates, World Inequality Report 2018 (Piketty et al.) via Our World in Data; top 1% share of pre-tax national income, WID.world via its official R package; government expenditure, Our World in Data historical series. Correlation between the top marginal rate and the top 1% share, 1960–2017: −0.72 in the US, −0.75 in the UK.

On the two vertical scales. The tax rate and government-spending lines read against the left axis (0–100%); the top 1% share reads against the right axis (0–20%), because a share that moves between 6% and 19% is invisible when squashed onto a 0–100% scale. Both axes start at zero and neither is truncated, so the top 1% line shows the true shape and proportion of its own rise — a genuine near-doubling in the US and a doubling in the UK — without the vertical exaggeration that a clipped baseline would produce. Read the two lines as two separate measured quantities that happen to move in opposite directions, not as one scaled to mirror the other.

Why not government spending. I tested that version first and it does not hold. When inequality bottomed out in 1978, UK government spending was at its historic peak (≈49% of GDP) and stayed near it until 1986 — the decline arrives roughly a decade after the inequality turn. US spending was essentially flat at 34–35% of GDP straight through the entire period of rising inequality and never meaningfully fell. That is why the faint grey line barely moves here: the state did not shrink much, but what it did with its tax system changed enormously. Top rates went 70%→28% in the US and 98%→40% in the UK across 1979–88.

How a tax change moves pre-tax inequality. These are pre-tax shares, so this is not mechanical redistribution. The established channel is the bargaining effect (Piketty, Saez & Stantcheva, 2014): when top marginal rates are very high, executives capture little of any additional pay they negotiate, so the incentive to bargain hard for it is weak; when rates collapse, the return to that bargaining rises sharply and pre-tax pay at the top follows. Caveat: financial deregulation, de-unionization and the end of capital controls arrived in the same window and also raise top pre-tax shares; this chart shows a strong and well-theorized association, not an isolated cause.

Mani, Mullainathan, Shafir & Zhao (2013), Science

The same farmer thinks worse when short of cash

The same farmers, tested once while still waiting to be paid for their harvest and once after · Tamil Nadu, India

Pre-harvest (poor)
Post-harvest (paid)
Source & notes
Source: Mani, Mullainathan, Shafir & Zhao, “Poverty Impedes Cognitive Function,” Science, 2013. Same farmers, tested twice: once while still waiting to be paid for their harvest, once after. The mills — not the farmers — decide when each farmer’s harvest happens, so this is a fair comparison, not farmers choosing their best moment to take the test. The researchers also checked the obvious alternative explanations — tiredness, hunger, having taken the test before — and none of them explain the gap. The size of the effect is roughly what you’d expect from losing 13 IQ points.

Wagner’s Law

Externalities and public goods are government’s job — and as countries mature, that job grows, not shrinks. The state should be strengthened, in resources and capacity.

The long run

And each one grew its state as it got richer

Government share of GDP vs. each country’s own GDP per capita, by decade

Source & notes
Pooled r = 0.90; every individual country’s own series correlates at r = 0.92–0.96. Source: government-expenditure share, Our World in Data historical series; GDP per capita, Maddison Project Database (international dollars) via Our World in Data; sampled roughly every decade from each country’s earliest available year through 2022.

Why a within-country design, not a cross-country one. I first tried the more obvious cross-country panel — recent GDP growth rate vs. change in government share, expecting the same pattern. It came back with the wrong sign (r = −0.40), driven almost entirely by resource-exporting economies whose GDP swings with commodity prices independent of any real change in the state’s role (Equatorial Guinea’s government share fell 195 points against 1,236% GDP growth from an oil boom). Excluding those extreme cases, the relationship doesn’t reverse — it just disappears. Growth rate and development level are not interchangeable tests of Wagner’s Law; this long-run, within-country version is the one that actually holds up.

Caveat. A rising government share is also consistent with explanations besides externalities and public-goods provision — Baumol’s cost disease (public services are labor-intensive, so their relative price rises even without more service being delivered), rising demand for social insurance in aging societies, and political-economy dynamics all predict the same upward trend. This chart is strong evidence that the state’s role grows as countries mature; it doesn’t on its own prove which mechanism is doing the work.

The cross-section

Richer countries run bigger states

Government expenditure vs. GDP per capita (log, PPP), 149 countries, 2023

Source & notes
Source: World Bank government-expenditure and GDP-per-capita (PPP) series via Our World in Data; all 149 countries with both indicators available in 2023. Fit: OLS of government expenditure (% GDP) on ln(GDP per capita) — R² = 0.136, real but noisy. Predicted share rises from 23% at $2,000 to 33% at $20,000 to 38% at $60,000. A single-year snapshot can’t separate income from everything else that differs between countries — institutions, history, resource endowments — which is why the long-run panel alongside it is the stronger test of the same claim.

State capacity financing needs tax revenue — but that revenue requires accountability and good governance

Same pattern for total government revenue

The answer to the title

The growth we want, in five tests

Not a rate. A set of questions to ask of any growth number before treating it as good news.

✓Does it reach the median household, not just the mean?Growth that lands entirely in the top decile is arithmetically growth and politically nothing.
✓Does it widen who gets to contribute?The Lost Einsteins gap is forgone invention. Equalising opportunity is a growth policy, not a transfer.
✓Does it protect people through the transition?Most of the world has neither a formal contract nor state coverage. Protection is what makes openness and automation survivable.
✓Is it financed by a state that can actually collect?Capacity requires revenue, and revenue requires accountability — people pay when they believe the money is spent on them.
✓Can the planet absorb it?Not one country has decoupled fast enough for 1.5°C. And within every country, emissions track income.

None of this is an argument against growth. Between 1988 and 2008 the gap between countries narrowed for the first time in two centuries, and hundreds of millions left poverty. The argument is that the rate alone stopped being a sufficient measure of whether an economy is working — and that every one of these five is a choice, not a constraint.

Data infrastructure

Several panels draw on the same recurring databases and compilations rather than a single citable study:

World Bank: World Development Indicators (WDI); Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI), 2025 revision; Poverty and Inequality Platform; INDO-DAPOER; the Lakner-Milanovic World Panel Income Distribution.

World Inequality Database (WID.world), via its official R package.

OECD: Income Distribution Database (IDD); Compendium of Productivity Indicators 2018, Figure 5.5 StatLink data.

Our World in Data, compiling: World Values Survey happiness waves; Gallup World Poll Cantril Ladder / World Happiness Report series; Global Carbon Project consumption-based CO₂ data; Maddison Project Database; government-expenditure historical series.

FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data): Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index (GEPUCURRENT).

ParlGov election results, merged with PopuList v4.0 party classifications.

Sources. Each panel carries its own citation and caveats. Across the deck: World Bank WDI and INDO-DAPOER APIs; the OECD SDMX API and the StatLink spreadsheet behind Figure 5.5 of the 2018 Compendium of Productivity Indicators; WID.world via its official R package; FRED; ParlGov election results merged with PopuList v4.0 party classifications; the Lakner-Milanovic World Panel Income Distribution; and IMF SDN/2023/001 for the traced Global Trade Alert figure. Where a number is estimated rather than pulled, the panel says so.
